content:
This section is bibliography, not argument. File pages 365 through 376 contain alphabetical reference entries running from Cole, Gay, Glick, and Sharp (1971) through Hendler (1994), with printed page markers visible at 596 (file page 366), 597 (367), 598 (368), 599 (370), 600 (371), 601 (373), 602 (374), and 603 (375). Because these are citations rather than prose, there are no central claims, reasoning chains, examples, explicit limits, or disagreements authored by Steven Pinker here. I will not invent them.

What the section does provide is a map of the intellectual landscape Pinker was drawing on, which is useful for a thinking-machine project as a reading list rather than as evidence. Entries relevant to representation and compositionality include Jerry Alan Fodor's "The Language of Thought" (1975) and "The Modularity of Mind" (1983), plus Jerry Alan Fodor and Zenon Pylyshyn's critique of connectionism (1988) and Jerry Alan Fodor and Brian McClaughlin on systematicity (1990), all on file page 370. Perception and mental imagery appear through Ronald Finke's "Principles of Mental Imagery" (1989) and "Creative Imagery" (1990) on file pages 369 and 370, and Ronald Finke, Steven Pinker, and Martha J. Farah on reinterpreting visual patterns (1989) on file page 370. Learning and constraints on generalization show up in Raymond J. Mooney and Gerald F. de Jong on explanation-based learning (1986) on file page 367, and Robert F. Hadley on systematicity in connectionist language learning (1994) on file page 375. These are narrow language-learning results, not established universal learning laws.

Semantics and grounding are represented by Jerry Alan Fodor's "The Elm and the Expert" (1994) and Hilary Putnam-adjacent work such as Hartry Field on logic and meaning (1977), both on file page 370, plus John Haugeland's "Semantic Engines" (1981) on file page 376. Memory, time, and structure over time appear in Jeffrey L. Elman's "Finding Structure in Time" (1990) on file page 369. Causation, goals, and reasoning are touched by Leda Cosmides on deduction versus Darwinian algorithms (1985) and on social exchange (1989) on file page 365, and Gerd Gigerenzer on ecological intelligence and frequency formats (1995, 1996) on file pages 372 and 373. Analogy and creativity are indexed through Ronald Finke's creative imagery work (1990) on file page 370 and Paul L. Harris on false analogies (1994) on file page 376. Emotions appear via Antonio Damasio's "Descartes' Error" (1994) on file page 366 and Paul Ekman on facial expression (1993, 1994) on file page 368. Social cognition is indexed through Leda Cosmides and John Tooby on social exchange (1992) on file page 365, Alan P. Fiske on forms of sociality (1992) on file page 370, and Martin Daly and Margo Wilson on kinship (in press) on file page 366.

Engineering implications, kept separate from any source claim: these citations suggest candidate mechanisms worth implementing and testing, such as compositional symbol structures à la Fodor, explanation-based generalization à la de Jong and Mooney, recurrent temporal encoding à la Elman, and frequency-based inference à la Gigerenzer. None of these entries demonstrates that a non-neural inspectable machine suffices for human intelligence or consciousness; the bibliography neither endorses nor refutes that restriction. The text is clean and legible throughout, with no garbled or visually dependent passages requiring uncertainty flags beyond normal citation typos.
